Few institutions have weathered the skepticism of the digital revolution with as much quiet resilience as the public library, and the case for their continued necessity is, if anything, stronger now than it was before the internet existed.

The first and perhaps most urgent argument concerns equity. The premise that the internet has democratized access to information assumes that everyone can actually get online, an assumption that crumbles quickly when confronted with the demographics of poverty. Millions of Americans lack home broadband connections, and millions more own no device capable of meaningful internet use beyond a basic smartphone. For these populations, the public library is not a relic but a lifeline. It provides free access to computers, high-speed internet, printing, scanning, and the full suite of digital tools that middle-class life now takes for granted. A teenager without home internet who needs to complete a college application, a recently laid-off worker who must file for unemployment benefits through a state's online portal, an elderly person navigating Medicare enrollment forms that have migrated entirely to the web — each of these individuals depends on library infrastructure in ways that expose the digital divide as a genuine and ongoing crisis. Closing or defunding libraries in the name of the internet's abundance is, in effect, a policy that punishes the people least equipped to absorb the loss.

Beyond technology access, libraries perform a social function that no digital platform can substitute for, because it is rooted in physical presence and professional human attention. Libraries have evolved into community anchors that provide job placement assistance, résumé workshops, GED preparation, English-language learning programs, small business resources, and tax filing help. Their children's and youth programming, particularly early literacy initiatives, constitutes some of the most cost-effective public investment in educational outcomes that any municipality can make, reaching families in the critical developmental windows before formal schooling begins. Equally important, and sometimes overlooked in policy discussions, is the library's role as one of the last genuinely open public spaces in American civic life. It is a place where a person experiencing homelessness, a retiree seeking company, a student without a quiet place to study, and a parent with a toddler in tow can all coexist without any obligation to purchase anything. The disappearance of that kind of unconditional public space would represent a serious impoverishment of community life, one that no app or digital service could repair.

The third argument cuts to the epistemological heart of what libraries do. A search engine returns results ranked by an algorithm optimized for engagement, advertising revenue, and popularity rather than accuracy, depth, or scholarly credibility. Professional librarians, by contrast, are trained to evaluate sources, construct research strategies, navigate specialized databases, and guide patrons toward information that is not merely findable but reliable and appropriate to their specific needs. This curatorial expertise becomes more rather than less valuable as the volume of available information expands, because abundance does not solve the problem of quality. The internet has made it simultaneously easier to find information and easier to encounter misinformation, and the librarian functions as a skilled human mediator between a patron's need and the overwhelming, undifferentiated mass of what is technically available. In an era of algorithmic recommendation systems that have been shown to amplify sensationalism and conspiracy, the professional library tradition of intellectual rigor and source evaluation represents a public good that civil society cannot afford to let atrophy.

Taken together, these three arguments describe an institution that addresses technological inequality, nurtures community cohesion, and defends the integrity of public knowledge — none of which the digital age has rendered obsolete, and all of which it has made more pressing.
